entry.title: cli: Log the performance monitor's readings only with -v (#1322)
entry.content:
cli: Log the performance monitor's readings only with -v (#1322)

`nsh run --fps` printed the performance monitor's line every second
(`perf Linux: fps 136/144 frame …`), flooding the terminal while the
panel already shows the readings. The platforms (Linux, macOS, Windows,
iOS, GPUI, TUI) now log that line under its own target, `nsh::fps`,
apart from `--trace`'s `nsh::perf` timings; the CLI shows NSH's own
lines other than `nsh::perf` only with `-v`, so the readings appear with
`nsh run --fps -v`, as `nsh test --fps` already documented. Docs
(`docs/dev`, website in English and zh-CN) and the CLI help say so.

## Public API

- `nsh_engine::perf::LOG_TARGET: &str = "nsh::fps"` — the log target of
the monitor's per-second readings.

## Breaking Changes

The monitor's per-second line moves from target `nsh::perf` to
`nsh::fps`; `nsh run --fps` shows it only with `-v`.

```diff
- log::info!(target: "nsh::perf", "fps …")
+ log::info!(target: "nsh::fps", "fps …")
```

## Validation

`cargo +nightly fmt --all` (both workspaces); `cargo clippy -p
nsh-engine -p nsh-platform-linux -p nsh-linux-host -p nsh-platform-tui
-p nsh-cli --all-targets`; `cargo check -p nsh-platform-gpui`. The
macOS, Windows and iOS backends were not compiled here (a one-line
target change each); not tried in a running window.

entry.title: core: Render far rows of an Each in a scroll view as they come near (…
entry.content:
core: Render far rows of an Each in a scroll view as they come near (#1312)

Builds on #1304. Content culling spares far rows their native views, but
each row's JS still ran and its nodes were laid out. Now, in a scroll
view that culls, an `Each` renders its first rows and leaves the rest as
placeholders, sized like the rows beside them. The core asks for a row
when it comes near, and JS renders it in the same commit. Engines that
do not cull (tests, test drivers, nsh-compat, the web) render every row
as before.

A 2000-row `<Each>` page on GTK (debug): the first commit takes 49ms
instead of 155ms, with 2194 nodes instead of 14 002, and the first frame
takes 55ms instead of 218ms.

## Validation

- nsh-core, nsh-js and nsh-engine tests pass, including new ones:
placeholders ask for their rows as they come near, the scroll position
holds when a row replaces its placeholder, and a 2000-item `Each` keeps
array updates right for rendered and pending rows.
- On GTK, rows show in place after scrolling 63 000pt down and after
scrolling 8000pt down and back.

entry.title: engine: Measure the performance monitor's CPU over a second (#1313)
entry.content:
engine: Measure the performance monitor's CPU over a second (#1313)

On Linux the performance monitor showed CPU near 100% on an idle window
after a scroll, though no thread was busy (the kernel's count for the
process agreed: about 15s of CPU over 2.5 minutes). The CPU reading was
the rate since the previous sample, and two callers sample the same
`ProcessSampler`: the panel's timer every 500ms and the frame its redraw
makes a few milliseconds later. So the second window covered one frame's
paint.

The sampler now keeps recent readings and reports the rate over the last
`CPU_WINDOW` (1s), however often anything samples. It reports nothing
for the first 250ms. iOS, macOS and Windows use the same sampler.

## Public API

- `nsh_engine::perf::CPU_WINDOW: Duration`: the span the monitor's CPU
reading covers (1s).

## Validation

- `cargo test -p nsh-engine --lib perf` (6, including a new
`cpu_is_a_rate_over_the_window`) and clippy pass.
- Gallery in release on GTK with `--fps`, idle after a fling: the panel
reads 0–1%, matching the process's CPU time over 10s in `/proc` (0%).
Before, it read 99–106%.

entry.title: macos: Picture a backdrop of only what draws under it, and only when …
entry.content:
macos: Picture a backdrop of only what draws under it, and only when that changed (#1316)

## What

Two commits on the macOS backdrop of a shader that reads
`sample_backdrop`:

1. **Picture only what draws under the reader, and only when that
changed.** The backdrop was the root with only the reader hidden, so it
held what draws over it (a light shader, the bar's own controls). It
also re-pictured on every UI-thread change: an animator write, a scroll,
a canvas redraw. Now it leaves out the reader and every layer composited
over it (`over_reader`), like Linux's paint. `ui_changed` marks a
backdrop only when the changed view draws under the reader and its
clipped drawn area meets the reader's box plus `overflow`. A picture
equal to the last is not uploaded.
2. **Leave out the trees that draw nothing where it reads.**
`renderInContext:` rasterizes every layer it is given. Under a bar over
a long list it drew every bound row. `shader::cull` hides, while the
backdrop draws, the subtrees whose drawn area does not meet the read
area. A test checks that the culled picture's pixels equal the whole
tree's.

Unsure cases are always pictured / kept: filters, non-finite
coordinates.

Pairs with #1315 (core stops sending `ShaderInput` for changes over the
reader); each stands alone.

## Data

`nsh test --target macos --fps`, Spotish demo: play a track, then scroll
the page under the frosted player bar. Opt-level 3, with #1315.
Per-second fps:

- **Before:** 21–100 fps, p95 often 26–45 ms; even the steady seconds
stay at 95–100 fps with 3–5% of frames over 8.3 ms.
- **After:** mostly 114–120 fps, p95 about 2.4 ms, 0–1% of frames over
8.3 ms. The dips (81–105 fps) are the seconds a new page's rows first
bind.

Profile after (rich demo, 30 s): most of the remaining main-thread time
is `renderInContext:` itself. This is mostly CG blurring the box shadows
of the layers under the bar. It is the next thing to address.

## Tests

- `cargo test -p nsh-platform-macos`: 108 passed
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -p nsh-platform-macos -- -D warnings`:
clean
- rustfmt on the changed files: clean
- Docs: docs/dev/macos.md, docs/dev/shaders.md

entry.title: core: Picture a backdrop again only when what draws under it changed …
entry.content:
core: Picture a backdrop again only when what draws under it changed (#1315)

## What

Every commit sent `ShaderInput` to every shader that reads
`sample_backdrop`, whatever changed. A frosted bar re-pictured the
window for changes that cannot show in its backdrop: its own controls, a
light shader over it, the tray, window attributes. On macOS and Linux
each picture is a render of the window on the main thread.

`mark_shader_inputs` now marks a backdrop reader only when a changed
view draws before it (`Core::draws_before`: an ancestor, or a view
earlier in draw order, siblings by `zIndex` then in order), or an item
shows everywhere (`shown_by`: appearance, tokens, tree order, and any
item it does not know). Items that change nothing in the window (input,
accessibility, desktop and clipboard commands, animated values) mark
nothing.

## Data

`nsh test --trace`, Spotish: open a playlist, play a track, 2 s of
playback (debug build).

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| ShaderInput items | 29 | 18 |
| small commits (≤ 10 ops) re-picturing the backdrop | 13 | 3 |

The remaining three are a pressed row drawn before the bar.

## Tests

- `cargo test -p nsh-core`: 1255 passed
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -p nsh-core -- -D warnings`: clean
- rustfmt on the changed files: clean

entry.title: js: Unwrap every accessor a NavStack route renders down to its screen…
entry.content:
js: Unwrap every accessor a NavStack route renders down to its screen (#1314)

## Description

Under `nsh run`, a route whose page is a component rendering another
component that renders the `<NavPage>` showed a blank page. `--release`
was fine. For example: `HomePage` → an app's page shell → `<NavPage>`.

In a development bundle, every component is a hot proxy, and a proxy
returns an accessor rather than an element. Two components therefore
give the stack an accessor around an accessor. `screen_of_accessor` read
only the outer one, so `screen_for` wrapped the inner accessor in a new
screen. The app's `<NavPage>` ended up as a screen inside a screen,
which no platform shows. Release bundles have no proxies, so the page is
the `<NavPage>` itself.

`screen_of_accessor` now reads every accessor down to what the innermost
component rendered. It reads them tracked, so a hot edit of any of those
components renders the screen again.

## How to Test

- New test: `cargo test -p nsh-engine --test engine
nested_hot_components_render_the_stacks_screen`. It renders a page
through two hot components and checks two things:
- The stack has exactly one screen, a direct child of the `Stack`.
Before the fix there were two, one inside the other.
  - An edit of the inner component renders the page again.
- `cargo test -p nsh-engine --test engine hot::` and `nav` pass. Clippy
on `nsh-js` and `nsh-engine` is clean.
- Checked in a real mixed app on Linux (GTK): the page was blank under
`nsh run` before the fix and renders after it.

entry.title: text_view: Avoid quadratic code-span searches in TeX preprocessing (#…
entry.content:
text_view: Avoid quadratic code-span searches in TeX preprocessing (#1308)

## Description

Avoid repeatedly searching the complete inline-code span list while
rewriting TeX delimiters in Markdown. With math enabled (the default), a
document containing `\(` or `\[` enters this path; a paragraph with many
code spans makes the lookup quadratic.

Consume the already ordered spans with a forward cursor. Advance past
starts skipped by a formula so subsequent code spans remain protected.
Add a regression test for formulas containing multiple backtick spans
followed by inline code, and record the performance baselines.

## Performance

Linux x86_64, Ryzen 9 7950X, Rust 1.99.1, workspace release profile, 11
alternating before/after rounds pinned to one CPU; medians. The
source-level harness uses the old and new real functions and checks
their outputs. Inputs are constructed outside timing; span generation
and output allocation are included.

Input: ``"`a` x ".repeat(k) + "\\(x^2\\)"``. Math is enabled and
streaming is off. Complete parsing includes Markdown-to-Document
conversion, with layout and drawing outside the measurement.

| Code spans | `latex::inline`, before → after | Complete Markdown
parse, before → after |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1,000 | 0.853 → 0.00891 ms | 1.548 → 0.795 ms |
| 5,000 | 24.366 → 0.0450 ms | 27.794 → 4.444 ms |
| 10,000 | 96.966 → 0.0914 ms | 100.688 → 8.911 ms |

The 10,000-span complete parse improves 11.3×. With streaming repair
enabled it takes 544.17 → 453.83 ms (1.20×); other scans remain. In a
35,200-byte control containing 200 short Markdown sections, TeX
rewriting takes 74.45 → 79.69 µs (about 5 µs more, a 6–7% local
regression confirmed in two repeats), while the complete parse remains
around 5.2 ms. Short Markdown and a 10,000-span input without TeX
delimiters have essentially unchanged complete-parse timings.

Headless `nsh test <entry> --trace`, debug, three fresh processes per
version against `bba76ef7`, with the same dense inputs in a mounted
`TextView` and an assertion that the text rendered:

| Code spans | First-commit median, before → after | Ops / mount items /
nodes, unchanged |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1,000 | 51.121 → 43.521 ms | 7 / 16 / 3,007 |
| 10,000 | 2731.507 → 1905.226 ms | 7 / 16 / 30,007 |

Counter control: initial 56 ops / 50 items / 21 nodes and `+1` 10 ops /
7 items / 24 nodes in both versions; commit medians 497 / 379 → 500 /
310 µs. These small control samples establish stable work counts rather
than a counter speedup.

## How to Test

- Passed `cargo test --release -p nsh-base --no-default-features --lib`:
315 passed, including the new code-after-formulas regression.
- Passed `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets`.
- Passed 3,375 differential combinations comparing both inline rewriting
and complete parsed documents.
- Passed the before/after headless trace runs for Counter and the
mounted 1,000-/10,000-span TextViews, three runs each.
- Ran the complete `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` suite. Its
only failing target is `nsh-platform-linux --lib`, with two failures in
unchanged code:
- `text::fallback_tests::fallback_fonts_keep_the_line_height`: emoji
height is 23 pt versus the expected 22 pt on this machine.
-
`decor::tests::cached_shadows_match_vector_drawing_and_update_with_their_inputs`.
All remaining targets completed successfully. The initial fail-fast run
also hit the CLI's port-reuse test; that test passed in the complete
rerun.

The changed Rust file passes `rustfmt +nightly --check`; `git diff
--check` passes. Whole-workspace nightly formatting reports existing
differences in the unchanged `crates/nsh-core/src/access.rs:1960` and
`crates/nsh-platform-linux/src/tray.rs:749`.

## Checklist

- [x] Read CONTRIBUTING and followed the project conventions.
- [x] Reviewed the implementation and its validation.
- [ ] Whole-workspace nightly formatting passes (existing differences
noted above).

entry.title: windows: Read window data only from the app's own windows (#1301)
entry.content:
windows: Read window data only from the app's own windows (#1301)

## Description

`window::data(hwnd)` reads a window's `GWLP_USERDATA` as a pointer to
NSH's `WindowData`, whatever window it is
given. Not every caller passes a window NSH made: the Windows test
agent's typing (`agent.rs`, `in_focused`) asks
`GetForegroundWindow()` which window has the keyboard and looks up its
app window root, and that window can be
another app's. When that app keeps a pointer of its own in
`GWLP_USERDATA`, `app_window_root` dereferences it and the
host dies with an access violation.

On GitHub's `windows-11-arm` runner, where other programs leave a window
in front, this ended the host in every
gallery test that types (`nsh test` reported "the host left"). On the
x64 runners there is no foreground window, so
the lookup finds nothing and the bug never shows. Symbolized, the fault
was `window.rs` `app_window_root` ←
`agent.rs` `in_focused`.

`data()` now reads the slot only for a window of this process whose
class's window procedure is `window_proc`, the
only windows `WM_NCCREATE` gives a `WindowData`; for any other window it
returns `None`, as for a window with no
data. `surface_of`, `app_window_root` and `shell` go through it, so they
all answer `None` for another app's window.

- `window.rs`: `data()` checks the window's process
(`GetWindowThreadProcessId`) and class procedure
  (`GetClassLongPtrW(GCLP_WNDPROC)`) before reading the slot.
- A test makes a window of another class with an unmapped address in its
user data and checks the three lookups
  return nothing instead of reading it.

## How to Test

- `cargo test -p nsh-platform-windows` (the new
`a_window_of_another_class_has_no_window_data`).
- On Windows on Arm (GitHub's `windows-11-arm`): the gallery's Windows
tests that type (`form`, `shortcuts`, …) pass
  with this change; without it the host exits during typing.
- The Windows clippy run and `cargo +nightly fmt --all`.

## Checklist

- [x] I have read the [CONTRIBUTING](../CONTRIBUTING.md) document and
followed the guidelines.
- [x] Reviewed the changes in this PR and confirmed AI generated code
(if any) is accurate.
- [x] Passed `cargo test` for the Windows crates on x64 and ARM64,
`cargo +nightly fmt --all` and the Windows clippy
  run.
- [x] Changes to what apps use keep what released versions shipped (no
API change).
- [ ] Ran the related `examples/gallery` demos on iOS and Android
(Windows only: not applicable).

entry.title: core: Make scroll views' native views only near their viewport (#1304)
entry.content:
core: Make scroll views' native views only near their viewport (#1304)

Apps often lay long content out in a plain `Scroll` instead of a `List`,
so every row's native view, text layout and image is made up front. With
this change, scroll views make the views of their content near what they
show, make the rest as it is scrolled to, and give far views back unless
those views hold state. Layout, `onLayout`, `measure()` and scrolling
from code still cover the whole content.

The platforms' apps turn it on. Engines started without it (tests, test
drivers, nsh-compat) mount whole content as before, so their steps reach
every view.

A 2000-row `<Each>` page on GTK (debug): the first commit sends 388
mount items instead of 38 008, in 155ms instead of 281ms.

## Public API

- `nsh_engine::EngineConfig::content_culling: bool`: scroll views make
native views only near their viewport. `EngineConfig::new` leaves it
off.
- `nsh_engine::EngineControl::set_content_culling(&self, enabled:
bool)`: turns it on or off on a running engine. Test drivers use it.
- `nsh_core::Core::set_content_culling(&mut self, enabled: bool)`: the
same, on the core.

## Validation

- `cargo test --workspace` and clippy on nsh-core, nsh-engine,
nsh-testing and nsh-platform-linux pass.
- On GTK, scrolling a 2000-row page down 6000pt and back shows the rows
correctly, and the views given up are made again.

entry.title: core: Bind a list's rows further ahead while it scrolls fast (#1310)
entry.content:
core: Bind a list's rows further ahead while it scrolls fast (#1310)

Dragging a `List` fast showed blank strips at its leading edge. Rows
bound for a scroll report show up a frame or more later, but only two
steps' worth of rows ahead of the viewport were bound right away, and
one slow frame shrank that reach just before a fast one.

Now the rows four recent steps ahead (at most the overscan) bind with
the viewport, and a recent longer step in the same direction keeps
counting, decayed, through slower ones. A turn or a jump starts over.

## Validation

- `cargo test -p nsh-core list` (107) and `cargo test -p nsh-engine
--test engine list` (31) pass.
- Gallery photo list scrolled 3000pt (`Bench.tsx`, release, headless):
43 commits, 2235 ops and 1856 mount items, the same as main. Steady
scrolling binds no more.
- In a GTK window, fast flings and wheel spins on the gallery's Photos
page no longer show blanks at the edge.

entry.content:
linux: Make the performance monitor concise and collapse it on a click (#1306)

The Linux performance monitor's panel had a heading, a footer and a
boxed chart with a budget line, and it covered the app with no way to
move it aside.

rows of readings: frame, p95, JS, core, CPU, memory, heap and nodes.

`bootstrap.js`.

No public API change, no new dependency.

the fix (2/2).
- `button`, `overlays`, `hover` gallery tests pass; `cargo test -p

entry.title: cli: Install other platforms' runtimes as components when needed (#1302)
entry.content:
cli: Install other platforms' runtimes as components when needed (#1302)

## Description

The release archives held every runtime the distribution has, so a
developer on one platform downloaded all of the others. Measured on
v0.4.0:

| Part | v0.4.0 macOS archive (gzip) | v0.4.0 Linux archive (gzip) |
After this change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `runtime/android` (release + dev × 3 ABIs × stripped libraries +
symbols) | 201 MB | 201 MB | components `android`, `android-symbols` |
| `embed/android` (the same `libnsh.so` again, already released as
`nsh-embed-android.zip`) | 109 MB | 109 MB | `nsh-embed-android.zip`
only |
| `embed/ios` (already released as `nsh-embed-ios.zip`) | 125 MB | — |
`nsh-embed-ios.zip` only |
| `runtime/ios` | 67 MB | — | component `ios` |
| `runtime/gpui` | 21 MB | 28 MB | component `gpui` |
| `runtime/web` | 13 MB | 13 MB | component `web` |
| `runtime/tui` | — | — | component `tui` |
| `runtime/macos` / `runtime/linux` (this machine's) | 34 MB | 39 MB |
**in the archive** (stripped) |
| `bin/nsh` | 22 MB | 24 MB | **in the archive** (stripped) |
| **Total** | **591 MB** | **413 MB** | **about 50–60 MB** |

The archive keeps only `bin/nsh` and this machine's own runtime; GPUI
and the web runtimes are components like the others.

This change makes a release archive hold the CLI and its own platform's
runtime only:

- **Components** (`crates/nsh-cli/src/component.rs`), as `rustup
component add` installs a toolchain's parts: `android`,
`android-symbols`, `ios` (macOS), `web`, `gpui` and `tui` are archives
of their own in the release (`nsh-<component>.tar.gz`, or
`nsh-<component>-<platform>.tar.gz` for one built per machine, each with
a `.sha256`). The first command that needs one (`--target android`, `nsh
package --target web`, ...) downloads it from the CLI's own release
(`v<version>` or `nightly`), checks its SHA-256 and its record
(`components/<name>.json`: the version and commit, which must be the
CLI's; a nightly CLI from an earlier night is told to `nsh update`) and
installs it beside the CLI. A checkout's build never downloads; it keeps
building its runtimes with cargo.
- **`nsh update`** adds the components that were installed again after
replacing the directory.
- **Release workflow**: `nsh component pack` (hidden) moves the
components out of `dist/nsh` into their archives; the components that
are the same everywhere (`android`, `android-symbols`, `web`) come from
Linux's build. The embedding SDKs are no longer in the CLI's archive
(they stay `nsh-embed-*.zip`).
- **Android symbols** are their own component, installed only on
request.
- **`xtask dist` strips the executables** it copies (`copy_executable`;
on macOS signed again ad hoc): about a sixth of each (`nsh` 59 → 49 MB).
It strips after the build rather than through the release profile's
`strip`, which would rebuild everything apart from the release builds a
checkout keeps for profiling.
- The Homebrew formula's test no longer packages for the web (which
would download a component inside `brew test`); it makes a release build
and lists the components.
- Docs: installation and CLI reference (English, zh-CN),
`docs/dev/tooling.md`.

Expected archives: `bin/nsh` plus this machine's runtime, stripped,
about 50–60 MB, against 591 / 413 MB.

## Components

| Component (`nsh component add <name>`) | Release assets (each with a
`.sha256`) | Holds (in the distribution) | Built on | Added
automatically by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `android` | `nsh-android.tar.gz` |
`runtime/android/{release,dev}/classes.dex`,
`runtime/android/{release,dev}/lib/<abi>/libnsh.so` | Linux | `--target
android`, `nsh package --target android` |
| `android-symbols` | `nsh-android-symbols.tar.gz` |
`runtime/android/{release,dev}/symbols/<abi>/libnsh.so` | Linux | never
(on request) |
| `ios` | `nsh-ios-macos-arm64.tar.gz` |
`runtime/ios/{iphoneos,iphonesimulator,maccatalyst}/` | macOS |
`--target ios`, `catalyst`, `nsh package --target ios` / `ios-simulator`
|
| `web` | `nsh-web.tar.gz` | `runtime/web/` (`nsh-browser.wasm`,
`nsh-dev.wasm`, `nsh.js`, `browser/`, `nsh-syntaxes.bin`) | Linux |
`--target web`, `nsh package --target web` |
| `gpui` | `nsh-gpui-macos-arm64.tar.gz`,
`nsh-gpui-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`, `nsh-gpui-windows-x86_64.tar.gz` |
`runtime/gpui/nsh-gpui-host[.exe]` | each platform | `--target gpui` |
| `tui` | `nsh-tui-macos-arm64.tar.gz`, `nsh-tui-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`,
`nsh-tui-windows-x86_64.tar.gz` | `runtime/tui/nsh-tui-host[.exe]` |
each platform | `--target tui` |

Naming: `nsh-<component>.tar.gz` for a component that is the same on
every machine, `nsh-<component>-<platform>.tar.gz` for one built per
machine, `<platform>` as in the CLI's archives (`macos-arm64`,
`linux-x86_64`, `windows-x86_64`). Each archive holds `nsh/` laid out as
the distribution, plus `nsh/components/<name>.json` (`{ "version",
"commit" }`).

Release assets after this change, in full:

```
nsh-macos-arm64.tar.gz         nsh-linux-x86_64.tar.gz        nsh-windows-x86_64.zip      # CLI + this machine's runtime
nsh-android.tar.gz             nsh-android-symbols.tar.gz     nsh-web.tar.gz              # components, from Linux
nsh-ios-macos-arm64.tar.gz                                                                 # component, from macOS
nsh-gpui-macos-arm64.tar.gz    nsh-gpui-linux-x86_64.tar.gz   nsh-gpui-windows-x86_64.tar.gz
nsh-tui-macos-arm64.tar.gz     nsh-tui-linux-x86_64.tar.gz    nsh-tui-windows-x86_64.tar.gz
nsh-embed-ios.zip              nsh-embed-android.zip                                       # embedding SDKs
install.sh  install.ps1  nsh.json  (nsh-release.json on the nightly)
```

## Public API

CLI commands:

- `nsh component list` — the components of this machine's release,
installed or not.
- `nsh component add <NAME>...` — download and install components of
this nsh's release.
- `nsh component remove <NAME>...` — remove installed components.
- `nsh component pack --out <DIR>` (hidden) — the release workflow's:
move each component of a distribution into its archive.

Release assets (new): the component archives listed under "Components".

## Breaking Changes

The platform archives no longer contain the other platforms' runtimes or
the embedding SDKs. An installed nsh adds a missing runtime itself; an
environment that runs nsh offline adds the components it needs
beforehand (`nsh component add android web`). Nothing apps use changes.

```diff
  nsh/bin/nsh
  nsh/runtime/macos/
- nsh/runtime/{android,ios,web,gpui,tui}/
- nsh/embed/
```

## How to Test

- `cargo test -p nsh-cli --bin nsh` (182 passed) and `cargo test -p
xtask` (8 passed), including:
- `component::tests::a_component_is_downloaded_checked_and_installed`: a
local HTTP server stands in for the release; download, SHA-256 check,
unpacking and installing, and the refusals of a wrong checksum and a
missing asset, leaving nothing behind;
- `a_component_of_another_build_is_refused`,
`a_packed_component_installs_into_another_distribution`,
`what_a_component_leaves_empty_goes_with_it`;
  - `dist::tests::a_stripped_executable_still_runs`.
- clippy (`-p nsh-cli -p xtask --all-targets`) and fmt are clean.
- The workflow's Package step, run as written on a stand-in `dist/nsh`
as the macOS and the Linux runner: the CLI's archive holds `bin` and the
machine's runtime only, the components and SDK zips each with a
`.sha256`, the shared components from Linux only.
- The CLI on the unpacked archive: `component list`, `add` of an unknown
name, the automatic add on `package --target web` / `android`, an
installed component used directly, `remove` leaving the core as it was.
- Not run here: a full `cargo xtask dist` and the Windows runner. Run
this workflow by hand without a tag (a dry run) to check the real
archives.
`runtime::gpui_uses_its_workspaces_cargo_output_instead_of_a_stale_cli_sibling`
fails on this machine on `main` as well, unrelated.

entry.title: android: End the composition when an input submits (#1300)
entry.content:
android: End the composition when an input submits (#1300)

Fixes #1285.

## Problem
`InputBox.setValue` holds a value that JS sets during a composition
until the composition ends. In a multiline input with
`submitBehavior="submit"`, the `commitText("\n")` submit path returned
early, before `super.commitText` and `syncComposition()`. A composing
span that was live at that point (e.g. a dictation panel) stayed in the
`Editable`, so the app's `value=""` after a send waited indefinitely and
the box kept the sent text.

## Fix
`submit()` (used by both the `"\n"` path and the editor action) now
removes the composing spans before it reports `onSubmitEditing`, then
runs `syncComposition()`. The composed text stays in the box and is
sent. `onCompositionChange` reports the end before the submit, as
browsers order it, and the value JS sets in reply is applied
immediately. If no composition is live, nothing changes. No public API
change.

This answers the issue's questions as follows. Holding the value still
applies to any live composition, but a submit now ends it. The live span
is committed (kept as text) rather than left to the IME. The JS clear
then calls `setText`, which restarts the IME input.

## Verification
- `cargo xtask android --dev` builds.
- Android 15 emulator (Pixel 8, Gboard soft keyboard), multiline
composer that clears on submit: typing `hello wor` and tapping the
keyboard's send key sends `"hello wor"`, the box clears, and typing
continues normally afterwards.
- Limitation: Gboard on the emulator did not expose a long-lived
composition (no dictation panel), so the emulator could not reproduce
the stuck state on `main`. The fix follows the code path the issue
identifies; a check on a device with a dictation IME would confirm it.

entry.title: desktop: Keep a focused view taller than its scroll view where it is …
entry.content:
desktop: Keep a focused view taller than its scroll view where it is (#1241)

## Description

A widget that gets the focus is scrolled into view (`scroll::reveal`).
For a span taller than the viewport the start won, so the scroll view
moved until the widget's top showed, however far that was. A web view
the height of its page inside a scroll view is always such a span. On
Linux it gets the focus from a click, and again when its context menu
opens and closes: WebKit's popover is its child, so focus in the menu
counts as focus in the web view. Scrolled to the end of a long page, a
right click moved the page back to its top, and the menu, still pointing
at where the click had been, showed in the window's top-left corner.

A focused span taller than the viewport that already shows now stays
where it is. It could only ever show in part, and moving it moves what
the pointer is on. A span that is out of view still has its start
scrolled in, and one that fits the viewport still shows whole, margins
included.

The rule lives in a new `reveal_focus_delta`, which the focus reveal of
Linux, Windows and GPUI (`scroll::reveal`) and of macOS uses.
`reveal_delta` keeps its start-first rule, which the TUI backend's
centered reveal builds on.

## Public API

- `nsh_core::scroll::reveal_focus_delta(start: Points, end: Points,
viewport: Points) -> Points`: how far a scroll view moves to show a view
that gets the focus; `reveal_delta`'s rule, except that a span taller
than the viewport that already shows stays.

## Validation

- `cargo test -p nsh-core --lib scroll::`: `reveal_deltas` covers
`reveal_delta`'s start-first rule and, for `reveal_focus_delta`, spans
that are taller than the viewport and show in part or are out of view,
and one that fits only without its margins.
- `cargo test -p nsh-platform-tui --test tui scroll`: 28 pass,
`horizontal_and_oversized_reveals_keep_the_core_margin_and_leading_edge`
among them.
- Manual check on Linux (GTK 4, WebKitGTK 6) in an email client whose
reader shows the message body in a page-high web view inside a scroll
view. Right-clicking at the end of a long message, and inside it while
its top shows, opens the menu at the pointer and leaves the page where
it was; closing the menu leaves it there too.
- The macOS change is not compiled here (Linux).

entry.title: bundler: Read import() of a backtick string as the module it names (#…
entry.content:
bundler: Read import() of a backtick string as the module it names (#1178)

Relates to #1039

## Description

An app that loads an NSH module with `import()` gets the whole engine on
the web, even when the specifier is a plain string. `nsh package`
bundles and minifies first, and the minifier writes
`import("nsh/desktop")` as `` import(`nsh/desktop`) ``. `NativeUse`'s
scanner (`natives.rs`, `visit_import_expression`) took only a
`StringLiteral` as a known specifier, so the template counted as
`computed_import`, and `linked_gates` then keeps every part.

A template with no interpolation is now read like a string (as `jsx.rs`
already does for JSX text). A template with `${…}` is still computed.

Found in a real app (Symbinote): one `(await
import("nsh/desktop")).Window.orderFront()` in a desktop-only branch
made its web engine 13.3 MB (2.9 MB with brotli) instead of 4.2 MB (1
MB). With a 300 ms server, 20 Mbit/s and a 4× slower CPU in Chrome, the
first visit took 2.37 s instead of 1.63 s.

## How to Test

- `cargo test -p nsh-bundler`: 70 pass. The new
`an_import_of_a_template_with_no_interpolation_names_its_module` fails
without the change; `` import(`./${name}.js`) `` is still computed.
- Repro on 0.4.0: an app whose `App.tsx` is
  ```tsx
  import { mount, View, Text } from "nsh";
async function front() { (await
import("nsh/desktop")).Window.orderFront(); }
  if (Date.now() < 0) front();
  mount(() => <View><Text>Hi</Text></View>);
  ```
`nsh package . --target web` gives a 13.3 MB `nsh.*.wasm`; without the
`import()` line, 4.2 MB. The bundled code reads `` (await
import(`nsh/desktop`)) ``.

entry.title: cli: Keep the generated crates' names short however many crates an ap…
entry.content:
cli: Keep the generated crates' names short however many crates an app lists (#1263)

## Description

An app with Rust crates of its own (`nsh.json` `"rust"`) gets a Cargo
workspace generated for it (`.nsh/rust`), whose
crates (`describe`, `test`, the hosts, the Android and web libraries)
are named after the app so they never clash with
the app's own binaries in its `target/`. With several crates, the name
joined **every** crate's package:
`nsh-app-<package>-<package>-…-<what>`. It grows with each crate the app
lists.

On Windows that breaks the build. An app with 12 bridge crates (found on
Windows 11 ARM64, NSH 0.3.0; the naming is
unchanged on `main`) gets a 183-character name,
`nsh-app-shell-bridge-feed-bridge-…-describe`, and MSVC's `link.exe`
fails with `LNK1104: cannot open file` on
`target\debug\deps\nsh_app_…_describe.exe` (264 characters) and on the
build-script paths under `target\debug\build\`. Windows' long-path
setting does not help: `link.exe` does not support
long paths. On macOS and Linux the same name runs into the 255-byte
file-name limit a few crates later.

This PR names the generated crates so the name no longer grows with the
crate list:

| Crates | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (`gallery-native`) | `nsh-app-gallery-native-describe` | unchanged |
| 2 (`charts`, `storage`) | `nsh-app-charts-storage-describe` |
`nsh-app-charts-ef5aa537-describe` |
| 12 (`shell-bridge`, …) | `nsh-app-shell-bridge-feed-bridge-…-describe`
(193 characters with the tests' names) | `nsh-app-shell-bridge-<8
hex>-describe` (38) |

- One crate keeps `nsh-app-<package>-<what>`, so single-crate apps (and
`rust-app.yml`'s
  `cargo tree -p nsh-app-gallery-native-…`) see no change.
- Several crates are `nsh-app-<first package>-<digest>-<what>`, the
digest being the first 8 hex digits of the
SHA-256 of the packages, sorted. The name is deterministic, keeps the
`nsh-app-` prefix that keeps it apart from the
app's own binaries, and still differs between apps with different crates
sharing a `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` (the reason
the old name listed them all). SHA-256 (`sha2`, already a dependency of
`nsh-cli`) rather than `std`'s hasher, whose
  output is not guaranteed across Rust releases.
- `RustApp::bin` is the only place the names are made; every caller (the
generated manifests, the Android
`cdylib`s, the web runtime's library, the TUI host, finding the built
binaries) goes through it, so they follow.
- An app with several crates builds once more after the update, under
the new names; the old outputs stay in its
  `target/` until `cargo clean`.

Docs: `docs/dev/rust-modules.md` and `docs/dev/tooling.md` describe the
new names and why.

No API change, nothing an app's TypeScript sees; nsh-compat records no
generated crate names.

## How to Test

- New unit tests, `cargo test -p nsh-cli --bin nsh
rust_app::tests::crate_names`: names for 1, 2 and 12 crates are at
most 42 characters (the longest, `rust-android`, included) and as long
with twelve crates as with two; they are the
same on every call and whatever the crates' order after the first; they
are distinct across crate lists and what
they are for; they keep the `nsh-app-` prefix; one crate keeps its old
name.
- The existing test of a two-crate app
(`the_generated_code_calls_the_entry_of_each_crate`) checks the new
names in
  the generated `describe` and `test` manifests.

- [x] I have read the [CONTRIBUTING](../CONTRIBUTING.md) document and
followed the guidelines.
- [x] Reviewed the changes in this PR and confirmed AI generated code
(if any) is accurate.
- [x] Passed `cargo test -p nsh-cli` (the tests above and `rust_app`'s),
`cargo +nightly fmt` and
  `cargo clippy -p nsh-cli --all-targets`.
- [x] Changes to what apps use keep what released versions shipped (no
API changes).
- [ ] Ran the related `examples/gallery` demos on iOS and Android (the
CLI's build names only: not applicable).
